report:
## Conclusion: the claim is supported, not false

The key evidence is MAP.3, a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 4,560 postmenopausal women at increased breast-cancer risk. At a median 35 months, invasive breast cancer occurred at annual rates of **0.19% with exemestane versus 0.55% with placebo** (hazard ratio 0.35; 95% CI 0.18–0.70): a statistically significant **65% relative reduction**. Thus, exemestane reduced *incidence* in the studied population.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/Nejmoa1103507

Important qualifications explain possible skepticism:

* The absolute short-term difference was modest (about 0.36 fewer invasive cancers per 100 women per year), and follow-up was relatively short; the trial was not designed to show reduced breast-cancer mortality.
* It applies to postmenopausal women with elevated risk—not average-risk women, premenopausal women, or all breast-cancer types equally. Aromatase inhibitors principally prevent estrogen-driven cancers.
* Adverse events were more common overall (88% vs 85%), although MAP.3 found no statistically significant between-group differences in fractures, cardiovascular events, other cancers, or treatment-related deaths during its follow-up.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/Nejmoa1103507
* Exemestane is **not FDA-approved specifically** for lowering breast-cancer risk, despite expert groups listing aromatase inhibitors as prevention options; “not approved” should not be confused with “ineffective.”  
https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/breast-cancer/risk-and-prevention/aromatase-inhibitors-for-lowering-breast-cancer-risk.html

The USPSTF likewise finds that aromatase inhibitors reduce invasive breast cancer in women at increased risk, but recommends individualized prescribing that weighs medication harms against baseline risk.  
https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/breast-cancer-medications-for-risk-reduction
